title: Arrested playing with Chris Kelly and as a boy
summary: He tells of a house-party job with Chris Kelly ending in a fight over pay and a night in jail, and a later arrest for playing sticks.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: No, no, I don't see that 5th Precinct. Let me tell you about that 5th Precinct, or the first time with the 5th Precinct. It was either the first time, the second time. I went there twice. Off and up, you know. That's right, I played a job with Chris Kelly on a court, it was a house party on a court between Maraday and Manifel. And, well, the pay wasn't much, I think it was a dollar quarter, the pay was about a dollar quarter. It might have been a dollar. But the people was giving us quarters, a nickel, a dime, you know, Tim was to play, you know, this tune, play that tune. And when we got off, Chris Kelly was dividing the money at the corner of Wakewater and Maraday on a light there. And Chris happened to give somebody a quarter too much. He said, I'm shocked, because I had so much money. And nobody had it. So they started a big argument, you know. And I thought, I didn't have anything to do with that. You know, I didn't take the water off. So I started walking off. I put my drum, my bass drum on my back. You know, those days you had to carry a drum, strap on the back and get a snare drum in the sack. You know, you had that, but a pedal and a cymbal, you know. And I started walking off. I walked the hitter. So they almost came to blows, you know. So when we reached the corner of a, before we reached the corner of a, a Quarton Frenchman, the two cops on the horseback said, line up. And I was like, I'm a little bit of a knife. I was like, I'm a little bit of a knife. I had a knife. I didn't have to cut no bottom of that knife. I just happened to have my pocket. And so I walked down, I was walking from Franklin Street to Gondonely. And over after Gondonely, we went, came towards Lizzie Field. So when I was on the track, I remember I had, crossing the tracks, I remember I had this knife. So I took the knife out of my pocket and dropped it on the track, you know. And so the caddies down on the fifth precinct. So the guy, I went, I asked the guy, the doorman, he knew me because he lived in the next block from me. So he said, what are you doing? I said, well, I don't know. I started a hard work. So I said, what do you tell him about? You know, my father, my mother, when you get off that, I'm here. She said, yeah, well. So I checked my drums. I checked all the guys at home and they put us right in the Black Mariah. They had two horses at that time, you know. They can't see nothing in the Black Mariah, you know. They put you in there and lock you in there. And they took us up to the nightcoats. So I get the nightcoats and all sitting there. I said, I'm guilty, not guilty of me. I said, I'm guilty of you. I told him, he said, you find everybody, two and a half or 30 days or so. And I said, well, I did have $2.25 in my pocket. I remember that very well. I remember that. So I put this in the cell. So one guy said, loan me a quarter because I think he had $2 a quarter. I don't know how it was, but he said, if you loan me a quarter, I'll get out of here. And I go tell you, your daddy or your mommy that you're in jail. And I said, all right. So I gave him a quarter. Everybody seemed like they all got out with me. So one morning, about 7 o'clock, my father came and he paid my fine. And I came on out. That was for nothing. And the next time I went to the Fifth Free Center, I was working at the St. Charles Hotel. I was running the freight elevator. And I was standing on a reported corner, a corner of a reporter. We used to take drumsticks and beat on them and lay the step at that particular corner, two on Murray Street. And we used to whistle and play the sticks. We used to play the sticks. We used to play the sticks. And the other boy I called Scala Brown, he had sticks. And he was pretty good and I was pretty good. And we all could whistle pretty good. Good whistlers. We would whistle ratty, ratty tunes, you know. So this particular afternoon, I didn't stop there very long. I was talking to some guy. And I was on my way to the library theater. And I had my, my fed at the theater, I think it was 10 cents. And I had a nickel for my Johnny Crook. And I was playing what? Johnny Crook, that's a can there. A flat piece of can there, you know. And two cops came up there. One of them, the name of the cops, I can recall that pretty good, was Jesse Youngblood. It was one of the cops. And I remember it was Peru. Peru. So when I seen nothing coming, so I knew to call him the reporter like I'm on. Miss Mary Overhauls, you ought to see. And I wasn't hit behind the door. So they came in and looking around. I was bound to hit behind the door. It looks like the door was open when I was in the corner. And when they came, he came and looked and said, is anybody coming here, Miss? I'll lay down. So she said, no I didn't. I said, yeah I am. So I said, yeah I am. I got scared.
You know, I don't know. What happened? So they took me.
And the other guy took the other guy's horse and was leading the other horse. And the other guy had me heist up like that. Passed right by my mama's house, you know what I mean?
And I said, okay, what are you doing?

I'm going to jail. And a guy had me heist up like that. It's like I had to kill somebody, murder somebody, you know what I mean? So my father, well he's driving, you know, carousel. And he was working on Legendfield, which we began. And they struck from, you know what it was, Dauphine and Legendfield, where Christian Music Club. I got it wrong. I got it wrong. Yeah, I can recall her. And my dad was working for Missy the Undertaker's name again. I'm not sure. Oh, it was a popular name. But anyway, well past then my daddy's here. So he told me he was born and stuff. They got my son born in the precinct. So I went and over all of them in the lab. So he came out and told me to go to the night court. I had to go to the night court. They released me, by the way. They had to go to the night court. So I went to the night court and the judge released me. But that's not the first time I had no, actually when I was a man I went to jail. But when I was a kid I went too, you know. Yeah, I played on the lady's step next door to my house, you know. Oh, you know about that. I don't have to tell you about that. You got that one now. No, I never did that for.
Oh yeah, you got that one now. I gave you that one.
